specAnchors.text: understand how metals can be arranged in a reactivity series based on their reactions with: water; dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid
know the order of reactivity of these metals: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold

primer.text: From Group 1 (Alkali Metals) you have already seen potassium and sodium react with water, and you know the reactivity series by name from the periodic table work. This note turns those reactions into a measuring tool: comparing how metals behave with cold water and with dilute acids, and using the vigour seen to place them in the order of reactivity.

modules.title: Reaction with water
sourceHeadings: Reactions of metal with cold water summary table
modules.opening: The chemistry of metals is studied by watching how they react with water and acids, and the observations place each metal in a reactivity series. With cold water the spread is dramatic: potassium reacts violently, sodium quickly, lithium and calcium less strongly, while magnesium barely stirs in water but reacts rapidly with steam. Zinc and iron react only slowly with steam, and copper shows no reaction at all.
keyPoints: Potassium reacts violently with cold water and sodium reacts quickly.
Lithium and calcium both react less strongly with cold water.
Magnesium barely reacts in cold water, yet responds rapidly to steam.
Zinc and iron react only slowly with steam, and copper shows no reaction.
Calcium with water gives calcium hydroxide and hydrogen: Ca + 2H2O gives Ca(OH)2 + H2.

low.restatement: Drop each metal into cold water and watch: the fiercest frothers are the most reactive. Potassium tops the violence, sodium and then lithium and calcium follow, magnesium waits for steam, and copper does nothing at all.
low.analogy: Like a row of kettles at different heats: the top metals are already boiling over, the middle ones simmer only when steamed, and copper stays stone cold.
low.examPointer: Quote the observations in order from the summary table; the ordering itself is the evidence the question wants.

medium.restatement: Each metal's vigour with cold water fixes its place in the upper part of the series: potassium violent, sodium quick, lithium and calcium progressively gentler. Magnesium's rapid reaction is reserved for steam, zinc and iron manage only slow steam reactions, and copper's lack of reaction places it at the bottom of the tested set.
medium.analogy: Think of a sprint race run on two tracks: cold water times the front runners, while steam is needed to time the middle pack at all.
medium.examPointer: For the calcium equation, check the balancing: one calcium, two waters, one calcium hydroxide and one hydrogen molecule.

modules.title: Reaction with dilute sulfuric or hydrochloric acids
sourceHeadings: Reaction with dilute sulfuric or hydrochloric acids
modules.opening: Only metals placed above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids, and the more reactive the metal, the more vigorous the reaction. Potassium and sodium are so high that they react explosively with acids, which is far too dangerous to attempt. For the safer metals, every acid reaction follows one pattern: metal plus acid gives a salt plus hydrogen gas.
keyPoints: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids.
The more reactive the metal, the more vigorous its reaction with the acid.
Potassium and sodium react explosively with acids, so they are too dangerous to try.
The general pattern is metal plus acid giving a salt plus hydrogen.
Magnesium, zinc and iron each form their sulfate with sulfuric acid and their chloride with hydrochloric acid.

low.restatement: A metal reacts with dilute acid only if it sits above hydrogen in the series, and the higher it sits the fiercer the fizzing. The products are always the same in kind: a salt of the metal and hydrogen gas. Every successful fizz is the metal taking hydrogen's place in the acid, which is why position on the ladder decides everything.
low.analogy: Like a ladder over a fixed fence: any metal standing above the hydrogen rung clears it, and the higher it stands, the more spectacularly it lands.
low.examPointer: State the above-hydrogen rule first, then give the salt-plus-hydrogen pattern, and finish with one balanced example; all three lines together earn full marks.

medium.restatement: Dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid tests the metals that outrank hydrogen: their atoms displace hydrogen from the acid, forming the metal's salt while hydrogen bubbles off. Vigour tracks position, from explosive potassium and sodium down to the steady fizz of magnesium, zinc and iron, each making sulfate salts with one acid and chloride salts with the other.
medium.analogy: Picture hydrogen as a flag sitting on one rung of the reactivity ladder: any metal above it snatches the flag from the acid, and the higher the start, the faster the dash.
medium.examPointer: Write one table equation correctly, such as Mg + H2SO4 giving MgSO4 + H2, and generalise the pattern rather than memorising every row.

glossary.definition: The ordered list of metals arranged by how readily they react, built from observations with water and acids.
The compound formed when the metal takes hydrogen's place in an acid, such as zinc sulfate.
Water in its hot gaseous state, which reacts with metals too unreactive for cold water.
An acid mixed with much water, such as the dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid used with metals.
The gas released when a metal above hydrogen in the series reacts with water or acid.

workedExample.prompt: a) Write the equation for calcium reacting with cold water. b) Metal X barely reacts with cold water but reacts rapidly with steam; metal Y shows no reaction with water or steam. Identify X and Y from the tested set. c) Explain why copper, silver and gold do not react with dilute acids.
steps: a) Ca (s) + 2H2O (l) → Ca(OH)2 (aq) + H2 (g) — calcium hydroxide and hydrogen gas form.
b) X is magnesium: it barely stirs in cold water yet responds rapidly to steam. Y is copper: no reaction with either.
c) Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids; copper, silver and gold all sit below hydrogen, so no reaction occurs.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Ca + 2H2O → Ca(OH)2 + H2. b) X = magnesium, Y = copper. c) They lie below hydrogen on the reactivity series.
